lessons.title: Calligraphy: the art of beautiful writing
objectives: Hold a pen at an angle to create thick and thin strokes
Write a short word or phrase in a decorative style

keywords.def: the art of beautiful handwriting
one movement of the pen or brush
an angular, blocky style of Arabic script
a clear, rounded style of Arabic script used in many printed books

teach.heading: What is calligraphy?
bullets: Arabic has styles such as Kufic and Naskh
teach.note: Show examples of Arabic calligraphy on screen. Say that the Qur'an is the reason Arabic calligraphy became so valued. Do not ask pupils to draw people. Pupils need a pencil, paper and a flat-tipped pen or marker if possible.

teach.heading: Pen angle
bullets: Hold the pen at a slant
teach.note: Demonstrate on camera. If pupils only have a normal pen, press harder for thick and lighter for thin. Misconception: you need an expensive pen.

teach.heading: Practising strokes
teach.note: Warm up like a sportsperson. Give 3 minutes for strokes on the page.

teach.heading: Writing a word
teach.note: If a pupil is not comfortable with Arabic, they may write in English. Respect all skill levels; the Arabic teacher may help.

teach.heading: Decorating our work
teach.note: Remind pupils that decoration must not make the word unreadable.

practice: Draw a thick line and a thin line.
Which style is angular: Kufic or Naskh?
independent: Fill a row with thick and thin strokes using a slanted pen.
Write a word in pencil and check the spacing.
exit: Write a short phrase or your name in a decorative style with a border.
Write two sentences about why careful handwriting matters.
homework: How can you make a thick stroke?
lessons.send: Practise writing your name in the best handwriting you can, three times.

lessons.title: Landscape: foreground, middle ground and background
objectives: Explain the three layers of a landscape
Use size and detail to show distance

keywords.def: a picture of the countryside or an outdoor view
the part of a picture closest to you
the part in the middle of a picture
the part furthest away

starter: Name the pen angle that gives thick strokes.

teach.heading: Looking at distance
bullets: Objects close up show more detail
teach.note: Show a photo of a landscape (desert, hills, fields). Ask pupils to point out near and far things. Pupils need a pencil, paper, crayons or pencil crayons.

teach.heading: Three layers
teach.note: Draw three horizontal bands on a board. Misconception: higher on the page always means taller; explain it means further.

teach.heading: Planning an oasis
teach.note: Sketch a plan in light pencil. Palms and water are plants and landscape so they suit our school guidelines.

teach.heading: Using colour
bullets: Sky gets paler near the horizon
teach.note: Model colouring the sky from blue to white at the horizon.

teach.heading: Reflect
teach.note: Pupils swap with a partner (in breakout or on camera) and name the three layers.

practice: Which looks bigger: a tree near you or far away?
Define calligraphy in your own words.
independent: Draw three layers of a landscape using lines to divide the page.
Add a tree in each layer, making them smaller each time.
exit: Complete a desert oasis landscape with colour.
Label foreground, middle ground and background.
homework: Name the three layers of a landscape.
lessons.send: Look out of a window or imagine a view and sketch the three layers.

lessons.title: Mountain photographs: tones and shades
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do faraway mountains often look paler and bluer than near ones?
objectives: To understand how artists show mountains using tones and shades of one colour
successCriteria: All: mix a lighter and darker version of a colour
Most: make a tone strip of five steps
Some: explain how tone shows distance on mountains
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: mountains of the world (Year 4 Misty Mountain, Sierra)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at mountains as signs of Allah

keywords.def: how light or dark a colour is
a colour made darker with black
a colour made lighter with white
a picture of land and scenery

hook.text: Why do faraway mountains often look paler and bluer than near ones?
hook.a: Air and haze between us and the far mountains make them look lighter and bluer.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And the mountains as stakes?' (An-Naba' 78:7) and 'And He has cast into the earth firmly set mountains' (An-Nahl 16:15). Mountains are signs of Allah's design.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: To make a shade of blue you add ...

practice.q: Mix the middle step of a blue tone strip.
practice.a: A mid blue between the tint and the shade.
practice.model: I do: start with blue; add a tiny bit of white for step 2, more for step 1; a tiny bit of black for step 4.

independent.q: Paint a five-step tone strip in blue, then paint three mountain layers: far (lightest), middle, near (darkest).
independent.a: A tone strip and a three-layer mountain sketch.
independent.model: The teacher paints the far mountains first.

independent.q: Extend: add snow with white on the near peak.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why do faraway mountains often look paler and bluer than near ones?
exit.a: Air and haze between us and the far mountains make them look lighter and bluer.

lessons.homework: Find a mountain photo with an adult and note the lightest and darkest parts.

lessons.title: Designing a mountain model to scale
lessons.bigQuestion: Ben Nevis is 1,345 m tall. How could we make a model that fits on a table?
objectives: To understand how to design a mountain model with a scale and a key
successCriteria: All: sketch my mountain from the side and above
Most: use a scale to plan the height
Some: add a key for features (river, snow, forest)
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: scale and measuring; Geography: contours

keywords.def: how size on the model compares with real size
a plan
explains symbols on a plan
a line joining places of the same height

hook.text: Ben Nevis is 1,345 m tall. How could we make a model that fits on a table?
hook.a: Use a scale, for example 1 cm for every 100 m: about 13.5 cm tall.

starter.q: A tint is made by adding ...

model.problem: Scale 1 cm = 100 m. How tall is a model of Ben Nevis (1,345 m)?

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: At 1 cm = 100 m, a 900 m hill is ...

practice.q: At 1 cm = 100 m, how tall is a 1,085 m mountain (Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa)?

independent.q: Pupil PDF: design your model: side view with height to scale, plan view with contours, and a key.
independent.a: A scaled design with two views and a key.
independent.model: The teacher draws a side view of 12 cm.

independent.q: Extend: what scale would make Everest (8,849 m) 18 cm tall?

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Ben Nevis is 1,345 m tall. How could we make a model that fits on a table?
exit.a: Use a scale, for example 1 cm for every 100 m: about 13.5 cm tall.

lessons.homework: Collect newspaper, a card base and masking tape for next lesson.

lessons.title: Base, frame and the first papier mache layer
lessons.bigQuestion: Why might builders use a frame inside a big model or building?
objectives: To understand how to build a strong frame and apply papier mache neatly
successCriteria: All: scrunch newspaper into a mountain shape and tape it
Most: apply one smooth layer of pasted strips
Some: keep the shape close to my design

keywords.def: the inside shape that holds the model up
paper strips and paste that harden
one coat of strips
flour and water glue

hook.text: Why might builders use a frame inside a big model or building?
hook.a: It gives shape and strength; the outside layers can then be thin and light.

teach.heading: Build
cycle: Tape scrunched newspaper to the card base

misconception.wrong: Soaking strips so paste drips and the model goes soggy
misconception.right: Dip, then run the strip between two fingers to remove extra paste

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Why remove extra paste from each strip?
options: So the model dries and stays firm
check.why: Too much paste makes it soggy and slow to dry.

practice.q: Watch the teacher lay three strips. How much do they overlap?
practice.model: I do: lay strip 1, then strip 2 overlapping by about 1 cm, smoothing out bubbles.

independent.q: Build your frame and add the first full layer (finish at home); leave to dry somewhere warm.
independent.a: A taped frame fully covered with one smooth layer.
independent.model: The teacher covers one slope on camera.

independent.q: Extend: note how your model compares with your design.
independent.a: One sentence comparing shape and height.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why might builders use a frame inside a big model or building?
exit.a: It gives shape and strength; the outside layers can then be thin and light.

lessons.homework: Let the first layer dry fully (1 to 2 days).

lessons.title: Second layer and strengthening
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you think we lay the second layer of strips the other way?
objectives: To understand how extra layers strengthen a model and how to shape ridges and valleys
successCriteria: All: add a second layer at right angles to the first
Most: shape a ridge or valley with folded strips
Some: explain why crossing layers adds strength

keywords.def: make stronger
a long narrow top of a mountain
low land between hills
lose water and harden

hook.text: Why do you think we lay the second layer of strips the other way?
hook.a: Crossing layers spread forces in two directions, like plywood, so it is much stronger.

starter.q: How long did your first layer take to dry?

teach.heading: Ridges and valleys
cycle: Fold a strip into a ridge
Press in a valley with a finger

teach.heading: Drying well
bullets: Warm, airy place (not on a heater)
Check it is hard before painting

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.q: Watch the teacher make a ridge. What did they fold?
practice.a: A strip folded lengthways and laid along the top.
practice.model: I do: fold a strip in half lengthways, paste it along the top line, smooth the sides down.

independent.q: Add the second layer across the first and shape at least one ridge and one valley; leave to dry.
independent.a: A two-layer model with a ridge and valley.
independent.model: The teacher adds a ridge on camera.

independent.q: Extend: write why the model must be dry before painting.
independent.a: Paint on wet paper runs and the model can go mouldy.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why do you think we lay the second layer of strips the other way?
exit.a: Crossing layers spread forces in two directions, like plywood, so it is much stronger.

lessons.homework: Leave the model to dry all week; check it is hard.

lessons.title: Painting shades and textures
lessons.bigQuestion: How can paint make a flat surface look rocky?
objectives: To understand how to paint a mountain model using tones, shades and textures
successCriteria: Most: add darker shades in valleys and lighter tints on peaks
Some: dry-brush texture for rock and snow
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on mountains in the Qur'an

keywords.def: the first layer of paint
how a surface looks or feels
painting with very little paint for a rough look
the lightest parts

hook.text: How can paint make a flat surface look rocky?
hook.a: Dry-brushing, dabbing and highlights catch the light like real rock.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And you see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they will pass as the passing of clouds' (An-Naml 27:88). Even mountains will pass away; only Allah remains.

starter.q: A shade is made by adding ...
Where are the darkest parts of a mountain?

head: Effect
How
rows: Thin blue line in a valley

misconception.right: Layers of tone: darker in valleys, lighter on peaks

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: very little paint for a rough look
check.why: Dry brushing catches only the raised parts.

practice.q: Watch the teacher dry-brush. What happens to the raised parts?
practice.a: They catch the light paint and look rocky.
practice.model: I do: dip, wipe almost all paint off, brush lightly over the surface.

independent.q: Paint your model (base, shades, textures, details); photograph it and upload.
independent.a: A painted model with tones and at least two textures.
independent.model: The teacher paints one slope on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add your key's features (river, forest, snow).
independent.a: Features painted to match the key.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: How can paint make a flat surface look rocky?
exit.a: Dry-brushing, dabbing and highlights catch the light like real rock.

lessons.homework: Finish painting and upload a photo.

lessons.title: Evaluate: how accurate is my model?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a model useful if it is not exactly to scale?
objectives: To understand how to evaluate my model against my design and the scale
successCriteria: Most: compare it with my scaled design
Some: suggest two improvements with reasons
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: measuring in cm and comparing

keywords.def: close to the true size or shape
judge how well it worked
find the size
make better

hook.text: Is a model useful if it is not exactly to scale?
hook.a: Yes, it can still show shape and features, but a scaled model lets us compare real heights.

teach.heading: What does 1 cm mean?
bullets: 1 cm on the model = 100 m real

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: At 1 cm = 100 m, if your model is 1 cm too short, the real-life error is ...

practice.q: Design 12 cm, model 10.5 cm. What is the difference and the real-life error at 1 cm = 100 m?

independent.q: Pupil PDF: measure your model, complete the comparison table, and write an evaluation with two improvements.
independent.a: Measurements, differences and two reasoned improvements.
independent.model: The teacher evaluates a sample model.

independent.q: Class gallery: give a star and a wish to two classmates in the chat.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Is a model useful if it is not exactly to scale?
exit.a: Yes, it can still show shape and features, but a scaled model lets us compare real heights.

lessons.homework: Show your model to your family and explain its scale.
